newsitem.title: CHINA: China grain stocks said causing purchase problems.
newsitem.headline: China grain stocks said causing purchase problems.

text.p: Large-scale shipments of corn to southern regions have failed to ease the strain of huge grain stockpiles in China's northeastern Jilin province, state media said on Tuesday.
Slack demand and bumper harvests had left Jilin granaries over-full, caused losses to grain enterprises and influenced autumn grain purchasing, Outlook magazine said.
Trains laden with 1,800 tonnes of corn left for Shanghai on Monday from Jilin's Tieling city, part of the 2.0 million tonnes the province had been ordered to ship south, the People's Daily said.

China's State Council, or cabinet, last August instructed Jilin, China's biggest corn producting area, to send the corn to relieve southern shortages and to empty the province's storerooms for autumn grain purchasing, the newspaper said.

But even after the shipments, the province had spare capacity for just 6.0 million tonnes of grain -- far less than the 15 million tonnes of autumn grain it was likely to have to cope with this year, state media said.

The stockpiles had resulted in more than 2.4 billion yuan ($289 million) in losses for provincial enterprises in the first seven months of 1996, up 1.1 billion yuan from the same period last year, said the magazine, which is published by the official Xinhua news agency.
The magazine attributed the huge stockpiles in the region to sluggish domestic demand for corn and two years of good grain harvests.
Jilin's grain output this year was expected to reach 23 million tonnes from 20 million tonnes in 1995, the People's Daily said.

Grain authorities in the province had called for stricter management of foreign grain imports to southern China and for policies to protect local farmers' interests and ensure they still had an incentive to grow corn, Outlook said.
China imported 440,000 tonnes tonnes of corn in the first 10 months, down 86 percent from the same period last year, customs figures showed.
Asked if the province would be allowed to reduce corn stocks through exports, officials of the provincial grain department reached by telephone declined to comment.
China suspended corn exports in late 1994 to try to combat falling national stocks and curb rising inflation.
